lore.title: The bird who stepped out of the margin
paragraphs: Before Rook had a harbor, he had a page. A librarian named Lumen found a small red bird drawn beside an unfinished route in an old atlas. Whenever someone asked a question the atlas could not answer, its little bird seemed to lean closer.

One stormy evening, Lumen left the book open for a stranded courier. A drop of lantern oil touched the margin; the drawn bird blinked, folded his paper wings, and stepped onto the desk. He could not remember an author or a destination. He remembered one sentence: A good route leaves the next traveler a choice.

Lumen offered him a name, a scarf, and a cream satchel. Rook chose the name because it sounded like a small beginning with room to grow. His red feathers and swept crest stayed as they had been drawn. His lantern was ordinary brass: it needed oil, care, and someone willing to carry it.

Rook settled in Lantern Harbor, where Pip delivered letters and Moss repaired crossings. He learned that helping did not mean arriving with every answer. Sometimes it meant listening to a bridge keeper, waiting out bad weather, or asking whose story had been left off the map.

The atlas still contains a blank page that will never fill itself. Rook carries it into worlds inspired by gardens and caravans, river cities, snowy libraries, and wide-sky towns. He travels by camel, boat, train, and plane. Each place lends him a friend, a question, and a different way to be useful.

He is a gentleman by his actions: he asks before entering, gives credit, keeps entrusted names private, and offers help without demanding gratitude. He can be nervous, impatient, or wrong. When he makes a mistake, he says so and helps put it right.

Dragons exist in these stories. Some are frightened; some hold a gate too tightly; one simply needs a quieter place to sleep. Princesses can be astronomers, engineers, and the authors of their own rescue plans. Rook never owns the people he helps, and being rescued never takes away their voice.

The worlds share one book, not one correct way to live. Their towns and adventures are invented. Their cultural inspirations belong to many living communities, whose real histories are richer than a tale can hold. Rook returns home with a map of invitations rather than a map of conquered places.
rules: Keep Rook recognizable: signal-red bird, two swept crest feathers, white eye patch, projecting beak, dark scarf, cream satchel, brass lantern.
Costume changes serve the weather or a host’s invitation. Hats and boots may appear in winter scenes; they never replace the silhouette or turn a community into a costume.
Local friends have expertise, choices, humor, and continuing lives. Rook is a visitor who helps and learns.
Every chapter resolves its central problem. An invitation may connect it to the next world, but the reader chooses when to continue.
The lantern lights a small area. It is never an all-seeing device, a magic privacy shield, or a promise that a product defeats every restriction.
Bridges and routes express care, choice, and checking a journey. Their materials do not stand for a ranking of VPN protocols.
No real nation, faith, ethnicity, or ordinary resident is a villain. Obstacles belong to fictional circumstances and characters.
No borrowed franchise characters, company mascots, national caricatures, sacred-text quotations, or unlicensed decorative motifs.
Names, letters, and homes remain private when their owners ask. Sharing is offered rather than forced.
Conflict is solved through listening, evidence, repair, collective action, and safe alternatives. No weapon instructions or dangerous repair directions.
Real history belongs in clearly labeled cultural notes with primary sources. Fictional dialogue is not legal, historical, or engineering guidance.
The tale is enjoyable on its own. Product architecture is explained separately, where accurate terms and limitations can be stated plainly.

worlds.title: Lantern Harbor
worlds.description: Rook’s home is a fictional harbor of roof gardens, couriers, libraries, and bridges. These ten adventures establish the friends and values he carries into every world.
worlds.travel: A harbor footpath becomes a caravan road toward the Garden of Many Doors.

chapters.title: The borrowed light
chapters.theme: Share a useful light
chapters.summary: Pip’s last letters need a light that Rook is willing to lend.

pages.text: The last letters were ready, but the harbor lighthouse was dark. Pip the rabbit courier stood beside the water with his mailbag, watching steps disappear into the night. Rook arrived carrying his small brass lantern. “I cannot see the path,” Pip admitted. Rook looked from the letters to the stone stairway. His lamp could not light the whole harbor, but it could help two travelers begin.
pages.scene: Pip waits with undelivered letters beside the dark harbor lighthouse while Rook approaches with his small lit brass lantern on the quay.

pages.text: Pip showed Rook his empty lantern. There was no light left inside it, and he did not want to guess his way through the dark. Rook listened before suggesting a route. Together they checked the familiar winding path toward the lighthouse. “Then we will find it together,” Rook said. Pip knew the doors; Rook had a useful lamp. Each brought something the other needed.
pages.scene: Pip holds an empty dark lantern at the harbor while Rook listens closely, with quiet buildings and water behind their conversation.

pages.text: They took the stone steps one at a time, keeping to the small circle of gold. Rook carried the lantern ahead, and Pip followed with the letters safe in his bag. At the lighthouse door, Rook passed the light to him. “Keep it,” he said. “Someone else may need you.” Pip accepted it carefully. A useful gift could continue its journey after its first owner stopped walking.
pages.scene: Rook carries the glowing brass lantern up the stone lighthouse steps while Pip follows with his mailbag, both moving carefully along the known path.

pages.text: By sunrise the lighthouse shone above the harbor, and Pip delivered the last letter at its door. From the nearby bridge, Rook waved to the courier who now carried a light of his own. Pip waved back before continuing his round. Neither friend had made the night disappear alone. They had shared a route and a lamp, leaving the next traveler two people who could help.
pages.scene: At sunrise Pip delivers a letter at the bright lighthouse door while Rook waves from the nearby stone bridge above the harbor.

chapters.title: The noisy market
chapters.theme: Choose what deserves attention
chapters.summary: Moss’s market stall needs quiet without losing the signs that help people.

pages.text: Moss made maps, but his market stall had become a forest of hanging signs. Ribbons brushed the counter, banners hid the drawings, and a mouse customer could scarcely see him. Rook stopped beside the crowded stall instead of squeezing through. “What would you like people to find here?” he asked. Moss peered around a dangling board. “A place where they can ask the way.”
pages.scene: Rook finds Moss the hedgehog and a mouse customer at a map stall crowded with dangling signs, ribbons, banners, and hidden route drawings.

pages.text: Moss tried to show a map through the clutter while the customer waited. Rook asked which signs were useful and which had merely accumulated. They agreed to loosen the unwanted knots and give the counter room. Moss steadied the work, and Rook used his wings to reach the hanging ribbons. Taking things away was helpful only when they knew what they wanted to keep.
pages.scene: Moss shows a large illustrated map through the stall’s hanging clutter while Rook listens and the mouse customer waits beside the counter.

pages.text: Rook reached toward a small blue sign bearing a compass. Moss raised a paw before it disappeared with the others. “That one tells people what I do,” he explained. Rook paused, then gave the sign a clear place above the stall. A quieter market did not need to become a silent one. The useful compass could help someone find Moss’s maps and begin a conversation.
pages.scene: Rook reaches toward the blue compass sign while Moss points out its purpose, with the stall’s remaining signs and map rolls around them.

pages.text: At last the mouse could reach the counter and ask for directions. Moss handed over a folded map, hearing every question clearly. Rook rested on the stall roof above the single compass sign and watched the conversation unfold. The market still had colors, neighbors, and voices. What it had lost was the clutter that stood between a mapmaker and the person who needed his help.
pages.scene: Moss gives a folded map to the mouse at the tidy stall while Rook rests on its roof above the single blue compass sign.

chapters.title: The bridge that waited
chapters.theme: A pause can be part of progress
chapters.summary: Tess’s train journey meets a damaged crossing, and the neighbors mark a safe detour.

pages.text: Tess the otter had a train to catch and a green backpack ready for the journey. At the stream, she found a gap in the wooden footbridge. Rook met her on the solid bank as rain darkened the hills. “Can we make it?” Tess asked. Rook studied the broken crossing before answering. Wanting to reach the station did not tell them whether this bridge could carry them.
pages.scene: Tess the otter with a green backpack meets Rook on the solid bank beside a damaged wooden bridge and a clear gap above the stream.

pages.text: Rook checked the first loose plank from solid ground. The wood answered with a crack, and he drew his wing back. Tess waited beside him instead of stepping onto the damaged bridge. Rook folded his map and admitted they needed another beginning. A pause was disappointing when a train was waiting, but a broken plank was useful information. They turned toward the known bank path together.
pages.scene: Rook checks a loose bridge plank with his wing while remaining on the bank, and Tess waits safely beside him with her green backpack.

pages.text: Pip and Moss joined them with boards and red ribbon. The neighbors knew a dry route along the bank where a short detour could be marked. Rook carried his share while Tess helped choose the turning toward the station. They worked with the people who knew the path, giving the next traveler clear markers instead of another guess. The original damaged bridge stayed out of their route.
pages.scene: Rook, Tess, Pip, and Moss carry boards and red ribbon along the safe bank toward a marked alternative path beside the stream.

pages.text: The marked detour let Tess continue by the longer way, and she reached her train. Before leaving, she waved from the safe path to the friends who had helped. Rook, Pip, and Moss stayed beside the stream to check the red ribbons for the next traveler. The first crossing had not become usable just because they wished it so. Another beginning had brought the journey to a good ending.
pages.scene: Tess waves from the red-ribbon-marked detour while Rook, Pip, and Moss remain on the safe bank beside the stream and the damaged original bridge.

chapters.title: The two bridges
chapters.theme: Check the far crossing first
chapters.summary: A letter must cross two bridges, and the first gate waits for a signal from the second.

pages.text: Pip showed Rook a sealed letter beside a harbor divided by a small island. A wooden bridge reached the island, and a stone bridge would carry the journey onward to Tess’s village. The far crossing still had scaffolding around it. “The first bridge is ready,” Pip said. Rook looked beyond its gate. One completed beginning could not yet give the letter a completed way to its destination.
pages.scene: Pip shows Rook a sealed letter beside the near wooden bridge, with an island and unfinished stone crossing visible beyond the harbor water.

pages.text: Rook rested a wing on the near gate and kept it closed. Pip waited with his letter while they arranged a check of the second crossing. “Then let us check the far bridge,” Rook said. Moss brought his tools, and he and Rook took the workboat by the safe route. They agreed that Pip would wait for their clear lantern signal before opening the first gate.
pages.scene: Rook keeps the near wooden gate closed while Pip waits with his letter, and the unfinished far crossing remains visible across the harbor.

pages.text: At the stone bridge, Moss and the crossing’s workers finished the remaining work and checked its condition. Rook waited until the deck was ready, then walked the complete path with his lantern. He did not stop at the part that looked good from shore. Only after the far crossing had been checked from end to end did he raise the agreed light for Pip to see.
pages.scene: Moss and the crossing workers attend to the stone bridge while Rook walks its completed deck with his brass lantern to check the whole route.

pages.text: Pip saw the gold signal, opened the near gate, and crossed both bridges. On the far bank, he placed the sealed letter in Tess’s paws. Rook and Moss stood beside them, with the complete route stretching back across the water. Tess thanked the courier and his companions. The letter had needed a good last crossing as well as a good first one, and all three friends had helped it arrive.
pages.scene: Pip hands the sealed letter to Tess on the far bank while Rook and Moss stand beside them and both complete bridges are visible behind.

chapters.title: The right material
chapters.theme: Fit the crossing to the journey
chapters.summary: Rook discovers why wood, stone, and iron each have a place.

pages.text: Moss set three little bridge models on the workshop table: wood, stone, and iron. Pip, a mouse neighbor, and Tess had three different journeys in mind. “Which is best?” Moss asked. Rook almost chose the grandest model, then looked at the travelers. A garden basket, a heavy mail cart, and a windy gorge were asking different questions. They would need to visit the places before answering.
pages.scene: Rook and Moss show wooden, stone, and iron bridge models to Pip, the mouse neighbor, and Tess in a workshop filled with crossing sketches.

pages.text: The mouse’s garden route needed a few steady steps across a small stream. Rook accompanied her over the short wooden crossing as she carried vegetables home. Its modest shape fit that journey. Pip’s loaded mail cart asked for a different route, and the broad stone arch gave its wheels room. Rook began to see why the answer could change when the traveler, place, and load changed.
pages.scene: Rook walks beside the mouse carrying garden vegetables across a short wooden footbridge with a handrail over the small stream.

pages.text: At the gorge, Tess’s scarf tugged in the wind while she and Rook studied a drawing from solid ground. They listened to the crossing’s experienced keepers before settling the plan. A properly designed and checked iron bridge later carried the long journey between the cliffs. Tess walked it steadily. The useful answer had come from this particular place and its requirements, rather than a material wearing a crown.
pages.scene: Rook and Tess remain on solid ground beside the windy gorge while studying a drawing of the planned metal crossing between the cliffs.

pages.text: Back at the workshop, the friends gathered around a map showing all three bridges in their places. Rook set his lantern down and listened as each traveler described what had helped. Wood, stone, and iron had all found a useful role, with their own design and care. Moss smiled at the models he had first tried to rank. “Best for this journey,” Rook said, leaving every other journey its own question.
pages.scene: All the friends gather around the map of three different crossings while Rook sets his brass lantern beside the workshop table and listens.

chapters.title: The book that opened
chapters.theme: Beginnings belong to their witnesses
chapters.summary: Rook returns to the atlas where he first stepped into the world.

pages.text: Lumen asked Rook to help move the library’s old atlas. Its binding had loosened, and a page caught on his satchel. There, beside an unfinished route, was a tiny red feather drawn in ink. Rook remembered the smell of lantern oil and the first evening he had stood on the desk. “Was I made to finish this map?” he asked quietly.
pages.scene: In Lumen’s library, Rook notices a red feather in an atlas margin while the librarian supports the book’s loose binding.

pages.text: Lumen set down her tools. “I do not know who drew you,” she said. “I know you came alive when someone needed help. Those are different questions.” Rook looked at the empty spaces. For a moment he wanted a neat answer more than the truth. Then Pip arrived carrying three very untidy stories from the morning’s deliveries. Rook made room on the desk.
pages.scene: Lumen speaks beside the open atlas as Pip arrives with handwritten accounts; Rook makes space between tools and unfinished maps.

pages.text: They repaired the binding with the library conservator’s help and added a pocket for new accounts. Pip’s first story described a route the atlas had missed entirely. Moss added a correction to an old bridge. Rook contributed the sentence he remembered from the margin. None of the additions explained his birth. All of them explained a little more of his life.
pages.scene: A conservator helps mend the atlas while Pip, Moss, and Rook place original accounts and corrections in a new paper pocket.

pages.text: That night Rook left the atlas open, but he no longer waited for it to tell him what to do. Lumen gave him a loose blank leaf for his travels. “Bring questions back,” she said. Rook folded the leaf carefully. His beginning could remain a mystery. Tomorrow he could still choose to listen, be useful, and tell the truth about where his map ended.
pages.scene: Rook folds a blank atlas leaf into his cream satchel as Lumen leaves the repaired book open beneath a warm reading lamp.

chapters.title: The keeper of names
chapters.theme: Ask before sharing someone’s story
chapters.summary: A helpful public map nearly reveals a letter writer’s private home.

pages.text: The harbor council asked Rook to draw a map of friendly houses where lost travelers could ask for directions. He began with places he knew from walking with Pip. Then a letter writer named Nell saw her small upstairs room marked on the draft. “I welcomed you once,” she said, “but I did not offer my door to every passing crowd.” Rook put his pencil down.
pages.scene: Nell points at her upstairs room on Rook’s draft map in a public workshop; Rook pauses with his pencil lowered.

pages.text: Rook apologized and erased Nell’s home from the public copy. He asked the other households one by one instead of assuming that kindness meant permission. Some offered their shops during opening hours. Others suggested the library or the quay office. Nell chose to help write clear directions from her desk, with her address kept off the page.
pages.scene: Rook consults shopkeepers while Nell writes route directions privately at a window; a public copy shows agreed gathering places instead of homes.

pages.text: Pip delivered the draft only to the people who had agreed to review it. They found an old opening time and a stairway that needed an alternative route. Nell’s careful directions solved both problems. When someone asked who had written them, Rook checked with her before answering. She signed them with her first name and smiled. That much sharing felt right to her.
pages.scene: Pip carries reviewed map copies while Nell adds her chosen first-name credit and Rook marks an accessible alternative beside a stairway.

pages.text: The finished map welcomed strangers without sending them into private lives. On the back, Rook wrote how to request a correction or withdraw an offer. Nell brought tea to the library launch and chose to stay. “A door can be friendly and still have a lock,” she told him. Rook tucked his own copy into the atlas, grateful for the lesson he had almost missed.
pages.scene: Neighbors gather around the finished map at the library; Nell shares tea while a correction note is visible on the map’s reverse.

chapters.title: The tower with wings
chapters.theme: Listen to the person you mean to help
chapters.summary: A trapped inventor already has a plan, and Rook brings the missing partner.

pages.text: Mira, the harbor’s wing designer, was stranded in the old watchtower when a storm damaged the stair. Rumor said she wanted a heroic rescue. Rook arrived below with a rope and discovered that Mira had already lowered a drawing. “Please find the tower keeper,” she called. “I need a proper inspection, a platform, and someone who can read these measurements.” Rook folded away his untested rope.
pages.scene: Mira looks from a watchtower window above a damaged stair, lowering a measured drawing to Rook rather than waiting silently for rescue.

pages.text: The keeper studied the plan and brought a trained repair crew. Rook carried messages between the safe courtyard and the workshop while Mira explained what had shifted inside. A frightened young dragon had sheltered in the tower shed during the storm. His tail blocked the crew’s cart. Rook asked where he would feel safe, and the dragon chose the empty boat house.
pages.scene: A keeper and repair crew review Mira’s plan in the courtyard while Rook speaks to a frightened small dragon beside a blocked equipment cart.

pages.text: With the shed clear, the crew set up their checked platform. Mira descended with her drawings in a waterproof case. She thanked the crew first, then Rook for listening. The dragon peered from the boat house, worried that everyone blamed him for the broken stair. Mira showed him the storm damage. “You were in trouble too,” she said. “That is not the same as causing it.”
pages.scene: Mira steps onto a checked platform with her drawings; Rook and the crew stand safely below while the dragon watches from an open boat house.

pages.text: At the tower’s reopening, Mira displayed a model wing that folded instead of fighting the wind. The dragon offered to carry empty boxes, and the keeper gave him a clear place to stand. Rook wrote the adventure as Mira’s plan, the crew’s skill, and a visitor’s useful errands. It made a fine rescue story, especially because its supposed hero had learned to share the title.
pages.scene: Mira presents a folding model wing in the restored tower courtyard; the dragon helps with boxes while Rook records everyone’s contributions.

chapters.title: The blank-page atlas
chapters.theme: A map grows through many voices
chapters.summary: The blank atlas leaf becomes an invitation rather than a demand for answers.

pages.text: Rook laid his blank leaf on the library table and wrote Places I have not seen. Moss wanted to mark every shore before Rook left. Lumen asked who would check those marks. They stared at a magnificent mountain nobody present had ever visited. Rook erased it. “A blank space can be honest,” he said. “An invented answer can send someone the wrong way.”
pages.scene: Rook erases an unverified mountain from a blank atlas leaf while Moss and Lumen sit at a library table with scattered route notes.

pages.text: They made a pocket for accounts instead of filling the page with guesses. Fern contributed questions about gardens. Pip wrote a greeting for another courier. Mira added a sketch of her folding wing, labeled as her own experiment. Rook promised to ask before copying anything he encountered. The leaf became lighter to carry when it no longer pretended to know the whole world.
pages.scene: Friends place questions, a courier greeting, and Mira’s labeled wing sketch into a paper pocket attached to Rook’s travel leaf.

pages.text: A visitor from the Garden of Many Doors heard the discussion and offered Rook an introduction to Sima, a courtyard librarian. She drew the route she actually knew and left the rest for the caravan leader to explain. Moss noticed how many hands the map would need. “It will not be yours alone,” he said. Rook grinned. “That is why it might be useful.”
pages.scene: A visiting librarian marks a known route to a garden courtyard while Moss studies the many names credited along the atlas leaf’s edge.

pages.text: They opened a small travelers’ shelf in Lantern Harbor. It held the atlas, agreed accounts, and a card saying that questions were welcome. The shelf’s first blank notebook belonged to nobody until someone chose to write. Rook set his lantern beside it for the evening, then took both leaf and lamp home. A journey had begun before he had traveled a single mile.
pages.scene: A new travelers’ shelf holds the atlas and an inviting blank notebook; Rook collects his brass lantern beneath a library’s open evening window.

chapters.title: The road out of the harbor
chapters.theme: Depart with gratitude and a way home
chapters.summary: Rook joins a caravan carrying questions, introductions, and a return address.

pages.text: On departure morning, Pip packed a letter for Sima and Moss packed far too many pencils. Rook checked the caravan leader’s meeting place before leaving the quay. He could fly across a yard, but not across every mountain and sea. Travel would take companions, rest, and more time than a brave announcement. Lumen slipped the library’s return address into his satchel.
pages.scene: Pip, Moss, and Lumen help Rook pack beside the quay; a caravan meeting note and the library’s return address lie atop his satchel.

pages.text: Beyond the harbor, the caravan leader introduced him to Aster the camel. Aster lowered her head until they could speak eye to eye. “I choose a steady pace,” she said. “Passengers who want a race can choose another ride.” Rook agreed. He secured his lantern where it would not swing against her and asked where the others preferred to stop for the night.
pages.scene: Rook greets Aster the camel at the edge of the harbor road, securing his lantern carefully while the caravan leader points toward a planned rest stop.

pages.text: The first hill hid Lantern Harbor, and Rook suddenly missed it. He almost opened Pip’s sealed letter just to hear a familiar voice. Instead he took out his own notebook and wrote what he wanted to tell his friends. Aster waited beside a shaded marker. “Home can travel with you,” she said, “without every private letter becoming yours to read.”
pages.scene: At a shaded road marker, Rook writes in his own notebook while Pip’s sealed letter remains in the satchel and Aster waits nearby.

pages.text: By evening they saw the garden world’s first trees beyond the dry road. Sima met the caravan at the courtyard gate and took Pip’s letter. Rook introduced himself without presenting a list of problems he planned to fix. “I have brought questions,” he said. Sima opened the gate. “Good. We have answers to some, and questions to lend you too.”
pages.scene: Sima welcomes Rook and Aster at a garden courtyard gate with leafy trees beyond the road, accepting Pip’s sealed introduction.

worlds.title: The Garden of Many Doors
worlds.region: A fictional world inspired by Iran and Persian cultural heritage
worlds.tagline: Water remembers the paths we share.
worlds.description: Courtyard libraries, living gardens, night skies, and caravan conversations welcome Rook. Sima, Nima, and Soraya lead their own community’s adventures; this invented world is a starting point for curiosity about diverse living cultures, not a portrait of every Iranian life.
worlds.travel: Aster carries Rook to the garden city; a shared caravan and a coastal ship carry his next questions east.

chapters.title: The courtyard welcome
chapters.theme: A visitor begins by listening
chapters.summary: Sima introduces Rook to a garden where every door belongs to someone.

pages.text: Sima’s library opened onto a courtyard full of voices, flowerpots, and a patient tortoise reading beneath a tree. Rook looked for the grand door he assumed every library must have. Sima pointed to the ordinary one he had just used. “People come through that door every day,” she said. “A welcome need not be grand to be sincere.” Aster settled in the caravan yard nearby.
pages.scene: Sima welcomes Rook into a leafy courtyard library; a tortoise reads under a tree while Aster rests beyond the open gate.

pages.text: Rook noticed a blue curtain across another doorway and moved toward it, hoping to explore. Sima gently asked him to wait. It led to a family room. She showed him the public reading tables, the garden path, and the desk where visitors could ask questions. Rook thanked her for explaining. An open library, he learned, did not make every neighboring room public.
pages.scene: Sima guides Rook toward shared reading tables and away from a curtained private doorway, with blue tiles and potted plants framing the courtyard.

pages.text: At lunch the neighbors asked what Lantern Harbor was like. Rook described Pip’s letters and the two bridges, then invited their questions. Nima, who cared for the garden’s water, asked about the stream beneath them. Rook knew less about that stream than he had imagined. He opened his notebook to a clean page and wrote a question to send Moss instead of making up an answer.
pages.scene: Rook shares lunch with Sima and Nima beneath courtyard trees, writing a question beside a sketch of Lantern Harbor’s two bridges.

pages.text: That evening Sima gave him a place at the travelers’ shelf. He put Lantern Harbor’s greeting there with Pip’s permission written on its envelope. Nima invited him to see the water channels in the morning. Rook had crossed a world without solving a single problem, yet his map had already changed: its newest mark was a table where a stranger had been allowed to become a guest.
pages.scene: Rook adds an agreed greeting to a courtyard travelers’ shelf while Sima and Nima point toward tomorrow’s garden walk beneath a warm evening lamp.

chapters.title: Four ribbons of water
chapters.theme: Understand a shared system before changing it
chapters.summary: A quiet garden puzzle is solved by its keeper’s knowledge, not Rook’s first guess.

pages.text: Four paths divided Nima’s garden, with water glimmering beside them. One bed of flowers looked thirsty. Rook pointed to the nearest channel. “Could we make this one larger?” Nima asked him to walk the whole garden first. They visited trees, a kitchen plot, a shaded pool, and the thirsty bed. The water served many places before it reached the flowers Rook had noticed.
pages.scene: Nima leads Rook along four garden paths with narrow water channels; one flower bed is dry while trees, a pool, and vegetables share the water.

pages.text: At the far corner, leaves had collected where the keeper could safely clear them. Nima arranged the maintenance and explained who depended on the flow downstream. Rook held a basket for the leaves. “I was ready to change the part I could see,” he admitted. “Seeing a little is useful,” Nima replied, “when it makes us ask about the rest.”
pages.scene: Rook holds a leaf basket as Nima works at a safe maintenance point, with downstream garden beds visible along the channel.

pages.text: Water returned to the flowers gradually. Rook watched impatiently, then noticed that the pool was settling and a child was counting new ripples. Nothing was broken because it took time. Nima asked each gardener to check their own bed before calling the job finished. A kitchen grower found another small obstruction, and the keepers added it to their maintenance notes.
pages.scene: Water moves back into the dry flower bed while a child counts ripples and neighboring gardeners inspect their sections with Nima.

pages.text: At sunset the paths looked unchanged, but Rook understood them differently. With Nima’s approval, he sketched their shared flow and credited the garden keepers. The drawing was a story about cooperation, not instructions for building a water system. Beneath it he wrote: Walk farther before moving the nearest stone. He sent Moss the page, certain that a bridge keeper would appreciate a garden keeper’s question.
pages.scene: Rook sketches the interconnected garden under a sunset lamp, with Nima’s chosen credit beside the paths and a sealed note addressed to Moss.

chapters.title: The letter in the wind
chapters.theme: A message needs a named destination
chapters.summary: Rook and a local courier recover a letter without opening it.

pages.text: A gust lifted a letter from Darya’s courier tray and carried it into the shade beneath a tall ventilation tower. Rook raced after it, ready to fly up through an opening. Darya called him back. She knew which doors led to safe public spaces and which passages were for trained caretakers. Together they asked the tower keeper where the paper might have landed.
pages.scene: Darya the courier stops red Rook below a wind-catching tower as a white envelope disappears into a shaded courtyard opening.

pages.text: The keeper brought the letter from an accessible collection shelf. Its outer address had blurred where a drop of water touched it. Rook suggested opening it to find a name. Darya shook her head. “The words inside are not ours.” They checked her delivery record and contacted the sender, who could confirm the intended destination without revealing the private message.
pages.scene: The keeper returns a damp envelope to Darya and Rook; Darya compares its blurred outer address with her courier record at a shaded desk.

pages.text: The sender supplied a fresh outer envelope. Darya placed the unopened letter inside and asked the recipient where it should be delivered. He chose Sima’s library desk because he would be there that afternoon. Rook carried the tray beside Darya, holding it level through the next gust. The tower no longer seemed like an obstacle; it was simply a place whose keeper knew more than a visiting bird.
pages.scene: Rook steadies Darya’s tray as she carries a newly addressed outer envelope toward the courtyard library, with the tower keeper waving behind them.

pages.text: At the library the recipient thanked them and opened his letter himself. Rook did not lean over his shoulder. Darya gave the keeper a secure tray cover for future deliveries, and he showed her where public notices belonged. The wind still moved through the courtyard. The new arrangement did not conquer it; it made a small, ordinary task less likely to go wrong.
pages.scene: The recipient reads privately at Sima’s library while Darya thanks the tower keeper and Rook fits a cover over the courier tray.

chapters.title: The carpet of routes
chapters.theme: Credit the maker and ask what a pattern means
chapters.summary: A weaver helps Rook distinguish admiration from permission.

pages.text: At the market, a weaver named Leila displayed a carpet with a border that reminded Rook of interlocking paths. He began copying it into his atlas, imagining it as a decoration for every future page. Leila watched his pencil. “Would you like to ask me about it?” she said. Rook closed the book, suddenly aware that he had mistaken admiration for an invitation.
pages.scene: Leila stands beside a carpet with a geometric border while Rook stops copying its pattern into his open travel atlas.

pages.text: Leila described her own design choices and the work of her family’s workshop. She offered to draw a small original travel emblem for his notebook, but asked him not to present her carpet border as his creation. Rook agreed and listened while she explained which story she wanted the emblem to tell. He did not ask her to speak for every weaver in the world.
pages.scene: Leila sketches an original small travel emblem at her workshop table as Rook listens beside tools and unfinished woven work.

pages.text: They settled on a simple lantern beside an open doorway, different from the carpet. Leila added her chosen signature. Rook paid for the work and wrote how it could be shared. When another traveler asked for a copy, Rook showed her the permission note first. Leila smiled at the careful answer. Her work could travel without its maker disappearing from the story.
pages.scene: Rook and Leila review a lantern-and-doorway sketch with a signed permission note while a traveler asks about the new notebook emblem.

pages.text: The carpet remained in the workshop window, carrying its own story. Rook’s little emblem traveled on a separate page with Leila’s credit intact. He later sent her a photograph from the road and asked whether the caption was right. She changed one word. Rook welcomed the correction; a beautiful mark became more meaningful when the person who made it could still speak.
pages.scene: Rook posts a small travel picture with Leila’s credited emblem; the carpet stays visible in her workshop and a corrected caption rests on the desk.

chapters.title: The well after sunset
chapters.theme: Leave difficult work to the people who know it
chapters.summary: A missing water delivery calls for patient coordination above ground.

pages.text: The courtyard’s water delivery failed just before supper. People gathered near the covered well, and Rook wondered whether his small size made him the best person to investigate below. Nima stopped that idea before it became a plan. Underground passages were not adventures for untrained visitors. She called the responsible water team while Sima moved the supper tables toward a neighboring courtyard with a working supply.
pages.scene: Rook stands beside a covered well with Nima while Sima directs supper guests toward a neighboring courtyard; the underground access remains secured.

pages.text: The water team inspected the problem from their approved work area. Rook helped carry sealed drinking water and wrote clear messages at the library entrance. He asked Nima what information could be shared and kept people’s individual requests off the public board. Families chose whether to collect supplies or ask a volunteer to bring them. Nobody had to explain a private difficulty to a crowd.
pages.scene: Rook posts a clear supply notice while volunteers carry sealed water through the courtyard and Nima coordinates with a trained maintenance team.

pages.text: The repair took longer than anyone hoped. Sima opened her reading room and offered stories while they waited. Rook told the tale of the bridge that waited, including the part where he nearly acted too quickly. Nima returned with an update rather than a promise she could not keep. “The team is still checking,” she said. People had time to adjust their evening plans.
pages.scene: Sima hosts a small reading circle in the library as Rook recounts his bridge mistake and Nima brings a calm maintenance update.

pages.text: By morning the responsible team restored the supply and confirmed the checks were complete. The neighbors thanked the workers and returned borrowed containers. Rook recorded who to contact next time, leaving out the access details that visitors did not need. The most useful thing he had carried that night was neither a tool nor a heroic idea. It was an accurate message delivered when people needed it.
pages.scene: Neighbors return borrowed water containers after the repair while Rook records public contact information beside a thank-you note to the water team.

chapters.title: The princess of dawn
chapters.theme: A rescue has more than one author
chapters.summary: Soraya’s tower plan and a frightened dragon turn a rescue into a shared repair.

pages.text: Princess Soraya studied the dawn sky from a tower above the garden. A storm jammed the outer door and frightened the young dragon Zephyr, who curled around the gate outside. Travelers called for a hero with a sword. Rook asked Soraya what she needed. “My caretaker, my notes, and a way to speak to Zephyr without shouting,” she answered from the window.
pages.scene: Princess astronomer Soraya holds her notes at a tower window while Zephyr curls anxiously around the jammed gate and Rook listens below.

pages.text: Rook fetched the caretaker and stood where Zephyr could see him. The dragon expected blame, so he hid his face behind a wing. Soraya lowered a drawing of the sheltered courtyard. “You may rest there while the gate is checked,” she told him. Rook held up the drawing, and Zephyr chose to move. The caretakers could finally approach without putting anyone in danger.
pages.scene: Rook shows Soraya’s courtyard drawing to Zephyr as caretakers wait at a safe distance; the dragon uncurls toward a sheltered garden space.

pages.text: While the caretakers repaired the door, Soraya directed the preservation of her damp sky notes from inside. Rook kept the dry copies under his satchel flap. When the door opened, she stepped out carrying her telescope herself. Zephyr apologized for blocking the gate. “You were frightened,” she said. “Next time, let us know where you need help.” He agreed to practice asking before curling around doors.
pages.scene: Soraya exits through the checked doorway with her telescope; Rook protects her dry notes while Zephyr speaks from the sheltered courtyard.

pages.text: At dawn they watched the sky together. Soraya named the figures she had invented for her notebook, and Zephyr named a cloud after himself. Rook wrote a rescue with no defeated dragon and no silent princess. Soraya checked the account and added the caretakers’ names. “Tell people I asked for help,” she said, “and tell them I helped too.” Rook gladly kept both sentences.
pages.scene: Soraya, Rook, Zephyr, and the caretakers watch dawn from a safe garden terrace beside a telescope and a jointly reviewed story page.

chapters.title: A poem with room
chapters.theme: Make space for voices without speaking over them
chapters.summary: Sima’s reading night welcomes both a public poem and a quiet listener.

pages.text: Sima planned a reading night beneath the courtyard tree. Rook made a list of everyone he thought should perform, then noticed Darya shrinking from her name. “I like listening,” she told him. “That does not mean I want the whole courtyard listening to me.” Rook crossed out the compulsory list and replaced it with an invitation people could accept, decline, or answer later.
pages.scene: Rook revises a performance list beside Sima’s courtyard reading circle as Darya chooses a comfortable listener’s seat under the tree.

pages.text: Leila brought a poem she had written about a loom’s pause. Nima brought a short account of a repaired channel. Another neighbor asked for a quieter seat near the edge, and Sima made one. Rook offered to read the opening, but asked how his pronunciation sounded before the evening began. Darya helped him practice one name until it felt like a greeting instead of an obstacle.
pages.scene: Leila and Nima prepare their own short texts while Darya helps Rook practice a name; Sima arranges a quiet seat at the edge of the gathering.

pages.text: When Leila read, Rook listened without turning every image into a lesson about bridges. It was her poem, and some of its meaning belonged to her alone. During the pause, Darya quietly handed Sima a note for next month’s evening. She might like to read then. Nobody announced it. A choice could grow best when it did not become someone else’s celebration too soon.
pages.scene: Leila reads beneath warm courtyard lamps while Rook listens; Darya privately hands Sima a folded note at the side of the gathering.

pages.text: After the last reader, the neighbors shared bread and discussed what they had heard. Rook copied only the lines whose authors wanted to share them, using their chosen credits. Darya’s note stayed with Sima. The courtyard’s silence no longer felt like a gap waiting to be filled. It held listeners, pauses, and ideas that might find words on another evening.
pages.scene: The reading circle shares food after the poems while Rook records agreed credits and Sima keeps Darya’s note tucked safely in her notebook.

chapters.title: The caravan of notes
chapters.theme: A group can travel together without moving identically
chapters.summary: Aster and the caravan leader help Rook abandon a hurried schedule.

pages.text: Rook prepared a splendid schedule for the coastal caravan. Every hour had a mark, and every mark looked impressively straight. The caravan leader compared it with the day’s heat, the travelers’ needs, and Aster’s steady pace. “This road is not your page,” she said kindly. Rook folded the schedule and asked how the group made decisions when conditions changed.
pages.scene: red Rook shows a rigid paper schedule to the caravan leader beside Aster and the shaded caravan yard before departure.

pages.text: They chose rest points together and checked what each traveler could carry. Darya joined them for part of the route, carrying letters in a secure bag. Rook offered to take it, but she preferred to keep her entrusted work herself. He carried shared supplies instead. Aster approved of the lighter, better-balanced load and let him know when one strap needed adjusting.
pages.scene: Caravan travelers distribute shared supplies while Darya keeps her secure letter bag and Rook adjusts a load with Aster’s guidance.

pages.text: A sand-colored haze delayed the next stage. Rook stared at his useless hour marks, then wrote an update for those expecting the caravan. The leader chose a known shelter, and everyone waited there. Darya delivered the update through the agreed contact when it was possible. Rook learned that arriving later with accurate news was kinder than arriving recklessly to protect a timetable.
pages.scene: The caravan waits in a known sheltered rest court while Rook writes a delay update and the leader observes the hazy road from safety.

pages.text: When conditions improved, they continued at the leader’s chosen pace. At the coast, a waiting family greeted their relative with relief rather than complaints about Rook’s schedule. He tore out the hour marks and kept the rest points, contacts, and corrections. Aster leaned down for a farewell. “You have learned to draw a road that can bend,” she said. Rook thanked his very patient teacher.
pages.scene: At the coastal caravan stop, Rook thanks Aster and keeps an amended route sheet while travelers greet waiting relatives beside the sea.

chapters.title: The window of stars
chapters.theme: Share an observation without claiming the whole sky
chapters.summary: A cloudy evening gives Soraya and Rook a different kind of discovery.

pages.text: Soraya invited Rook back to the observatory before his ship departed. He expected a sky full of stars and found a roof full of clouds. Soraya did not pretend the telescope could see through everything. They checked the forecast, secured the equipment, and opened her older notebooks instead. Each page named when an observation had been made and what she had actually seen.
pages.scene: Soraya and Rook stand beside a covered telescope beneath clouds, then turn toward dated observation notebooks inside the tower room.

pages.text: One drawing left a corner empty. Rook reached to fill it with a familiar star pattern from Lantern Harbor. Soraya stopped his pencil. That part of the sky had been hidden on the night of her observation. His remembered pattern might be beautiful, but it did not belong in her record as something she had seen. Rook added it to a separate sketch and labeled the difference.
pages.scene: Soraya points to an honestly blank corner of a notebook while Rook moves his remembered star pattern onto a separate labeled sketch.

pages.text: Zephyr arrived with a cloud drawing of his own. It looked very little like the actual clouds, and he said so cheerfully. They made a small exhibit with two shelves: observations and imaginings. Visitors could enjoy both without confusing them. Rook added a fanciful harbor constellation shaped like Pip’s mailbag, while Soraya carefully kept her measured work on its own shelf.
pages.scene: Zephyr presents a playful cloud drawing as Soraya and Rook arrange separate shelves for observed sky records and clearly labeled imaginative pictures.

pages.text: Just before closing, a gap appeared overhead. Soraya let Rook look through the properly set telescope and showed him one bright point. One was enough for the evening. He thanked her for the real glimpse and the honest clouds. In the morning he carried a permitted copy of her exhibit labels to his ship, ready to notice where his next view would also end.
pages.scene: Rook views one bright point through Soraya’s prepared telescope as a small cloud gap opens above the garden tower and Zephyr watches quietly.

chapters.title: The sea between pages
chapters.theme: Carry introductions rather than assumptions
chapters.summary: Rook leaves the garden with a friendship that can travel by sea.

pages.text: At the coastal quay, Sima handed Rook a letter for Mei, a printer in the river world. “She helped us exchange books,” Sima explained. Rook asked what he should say about the garden. “Tell her what you experienced,” Sima said. “Leave room for what you did not.” The ship captain checked his ticket and showed him where to secure his lantern for the crossing.
pages.scene: Sima gives Rook a sealed introduction at a coastal quay while the captain indicates a safe place for the brass lantern aboard the ship.

pages.text: Aster had brought him as far as the port and would return with the caravan. Rook thanked her before boarding. Nima sent a drawing of the four garden paths with its keepers’ credits, and Leila sent permission to share her small travel emblem. The satchel felt full of names rather than souvenirs. Rook checked that each account still carried the choice of its maker.
pages.scene: Rook says farewell to Aster beside the gangway, checking credited drawings and permission notes in his satchel while the caravan prepares to return.

pages.text: The ship’s first night was rough enough to make reading difficult. Rook stayed in the safe passenger area and listened to the crew’s announcements. Another traveler wanted reassurance that the ocean would become calm at once. Rook could offer company, but not that promise. They shared a story of a waiting bridge, then rested while the people responsible for the ship did their work.
pages.scene: Rook and another traveler sit in a secure passenger cabin with the lantern fastened nearby while rain moves outside the window and a crew notice hangs clearly.

pages.text: Morning revealed a river mouth lined with busy boats and green banks. Mei met the ship beside the customs hall and took Sima’s introduction. “You have come a long way,” she said. Rook looked back toward the water. “With a great many people’s help.” Mei smiled and led him toward the city. The garden remained in his atlas, and the river offered a fresh blank page.
pages.scene: Mei welcomes Rook at a busy river port, receiving Sima’s letter as green banks and river boats open beyond the passenger hall.

worlds.title: The River of Returning Lanterns
worlds.region: A fictional world inspired by China’s varied river, craft, and urban traditions
worlds.description: A lively river city welcomes Rook among workshops, covered crossings, printers, ferries, and roof gardens. Mei, Lin, and Shen know this place better than their visitor. Old crafts and contemporary city life share the same horizon; this world never claims to represent all of China.
worlds.travel: A coastal ship brings Rook upriver; a northbound passenger train leads him toward the Snowbound Library.

chapters.title: The river welcome
chapters.theme: Learn the local signs before following them
chapters.summary: Mei helps Rook find a meeting place without assuming every sign speaks his language.

pages.text: The river city seemed to have a boat for every purpose. Rook followed a lantern symbol toward what he thought was Mei’s workshop and reached a festival storage room instead. The attendant kindly redirected him to the agreed meeting desk. Rook waited there, embarrassed but safe. Mei arrived carrying a blue umbrella. “You found a picture,” she said, “but not yet its meaning here.”
pages.scene: Rook waits at a river-port information desk after mistaking a festival lantern sign for Mei’s workshop marker; Mei arrives with a blue umbrella.

pages.text: Mei walked him to the printing street and explained the route symbols used on the public map. Rook repeated the meeting place back to make sure he had understood. A shopkeeper offered directions with a sketch when words became difficult. Rook did not pretend he could read every notice. He thanked her and kept the verified sketch, including the desk where he could ask again.
pages.scene: Mei and a shopkeeper help Rook compare a public route map with a simple verified sketch beside a busy printing street.

pages.text: At the workshop, Mei opened Sima’s letter and recognized Leila’s little travel emblem on Rook’s notebook. They set the introductions beside a kettle and compared the books that had traveled between their libraries. Rook saw how much work had happened before his arrival. He was following friendships, not discovering a place that had somehow waited for him to put it on a map.
pages.scene: Mei reads Sima’s introduction at the workshop table while Rook sets down Leila’s credited notebook and shared books beside a kettle.

pages.text: By evening Rook could find the workshop from the meeting desk without guessing. Mei let him print a small card with the agreed route and his own return contact. He left room for corrections as always. Outside, festival lanterns rose over the water for their actual purpose. Rook enjoyed them more now that he no longer needed every beautiful symbol to point toward himself.
pages.scene: Rook holds a newly printed contact-and-route card as festival lanterns glow above the river and Mei closes her workshop for the evening.

chapters.title: The bridge of many hands
chapters.theme: Value living skills and their keepers
chapters.summary: Lin’s covered bridge teaches Rook how a craft survives through shared care.

pages.text: Lin met Rook at a covered wooden bridge whose frame looked to him like lines woven together. He wanted to call it ancient and leave the description there. Lin introduced the people repairing a worn section, including a young apprentice studying beside her teacher. “It has a history,” she said, “and it has a working morning.” Rook watched from the permitted viewing area.
pages.scene: Lin guides Rook to a covered wooden arch bridge where experienced craftworkers and an apprentice inspect a closed maintenance section from safe work areas.

pages.text: The apprentice asked her teacher why an older record differed from what they found today. Rook expected the teacher to be offended. Instead she brought out another notebook and compared the repair history. The bridge had changed through many caretakers’ work. Lin explained that keeping a craft alive involved questions, training, and good records, not asking every young person to repeat without understanding.
pages.scene: An apprentice and teacher compare repair notebooks beside the bridge frame while Rook and Lin observe from a public path.

pages.text: Rook offered his lantern when a cloud darkened the viewing space, but the crew had appropriate work lights already. He found a more useful task helping Lin redirect visitors around the closed section. A child asked who had built the bridge. They read the public history together, including the names of current caretakers. The answer belonged to generations and to the people working that very day.
pages.scene: Rook and Lin direct visitors toward an agreed detour while the bridge crew uses its own work lights and a child reads the public history panel.

pages.text: After the authorized inspection, the bridge reopened. Lin invited Rook to record a story with the crew’s agreement. He described the apprentice’s question as carefully as the elegant frame. Back at Mei’s workshop, they printed copies for the caretakers to review. Rook’s atlas gained a bridge that was more than a pretty outline: it carried learning, labor, and a place for the next pair of hands.
pages.scene: Visitors cross the reopened bridge while Rook and Lin present a reviewed story copy to the teacher and apprentice beneath the covered frame.

chapters.title: The printer’s missing dot
chapters.theme: Check meaning before sending a message
chapters.summary: A tiny printing error nearly sends visitors to a closed crossing.

pages.text: Mei was preparing a booklet for the river festival when Rook spotted a handsome route page. He offered to deliver the first stack at once. Mei asked him to read the route aloud first. A small mark had vanished during printing, changing a clear instruction into a confusing one. The page looked finished, but visitors might follow it toward the bridge’s closed maintenance entrance.
pages.scene: Mei and Rook inspect a freshly printed festival route page at the workshop, with a small missing mark highlighted beside a closed-crossing sketch.

pages.text: They paused distribution and asked Lin to check the route wording. Rook counted the copies already placed in the public tray and collected them before anyone left with one. Mei marked the defective stack for recycling. Nobody blamed the apprentice who had first set the page. The error had passed several eyes, and their shared check had caught it while a correction was still easy.
pages.scene: Rook gathers unissued booklets from a public tray while Mei marks a defective stack and Lin reviews the route wording with the workshop team.

pages.text: The corrected booklet included the bridge’s opening times and a contact for updates. Mei asked a reader who had not worked on it to test the instructions from the meeting desk. He returned with a suggestion about a confusing turn. Rook revised the drawing, then tested it again. The handsome border remained, but the clearer route was what finally made the page ready.
pages.scene: An independent reader follows the revised route from the information desk while Rook improves a confusing turn on the workshop’s proof copy.

pages.text: At the festival, a family used the booklet to reach the right entrance and thanked the printing team. Rook thought of all the people who would never hear about the missing mark. That was a satisfactory ending. He put one corrected copy in his atlas and wrote the date beside it. A message did not need to be dramatic; it needed to mean what its makers intended.
pages.scene: A family follows the corrected festival booklet to an open river entrance while Rook dates his retained copy beside Mei’s printing table.

chapters.title: The flute and the flag
chapters.theme: A shared signal should reach its audience
chapters.summary: Rook discovers that hearing a sound is not the only way to receive a welcome.

pages.text: At a riverside rehearsal, a musician played a short tune to announce the storyteller’s arrival. Rook heard it twice as an echo returned from the opposite wall and began the introduction too early. The storyteller laughed and waited. Nearby, a visitor who did not hear the tune asked why everyone had moved at once. The welcome had reached some people and confused others.
pages.scene: Rook begins too early at a riverside rehearsal as a musician’s tune echoes from a wall and a visitor asks about the gathering’s signal.

pages.text: The organizers asked the visitors what would help. They agreed on a visible flag and a clear written start time alongside the music. Rook offered to raise the flag, but practiced with the storyteller first so the movement matched the actual beginning. The musician kept the tune; adding another signal did not require taking someone’s art away.
pages.scene: Visitors and organizers choose a visible flag and written start time while Rook practices raising the flag with the storyteller and musician.

pages.text: During the performance, a breeze tugged the flag out of place. Rook nearly chased it into the busy quay, then stopped and asked a steward for help. They reset it from a safe position. The storyteller paused long enough for everyone to find the next page. Nobody lost their place merely because one signal had failed for a moment.
pages.scene: A steward helps Rook reset the wind-tugged flag from a safe position while the storyteller pauses beside a clearly visible page marker.

pages.text: Afterward the visitor thanked the organizers for asking instead of guessing. Rook wrote a note beside his lantern signal from Lantern Harbor: Who can receive this, and how do we know? Mei printed the note for the festival team, who added their own ideas. The river still carried echoes, music, and wind. The welcome now had more than one way to arrive.
pages.scene: Rook and the festival team add their own ideas to a printed signal note while music and lantern reflections drift across the evening river.

chapters.title: The dragon at the rain pavilion
chapters.theme: Fear can hide a request for quiet
chapters.summary: A restless dragon and busy neighbors find room for one another.

pages.text: A dragon named Willow rested beneath a river pavilion during the festival. Whenever drums sounded nearby, her tail swept across the footpath. Some visitors called her unfriendly. Lin knew that Willow had asked for a quieter resting place before the festival began, but the message had been lost. Rook approached where she could see him and asked whether they could talk without the drums.
pages.scene: Willow, a long gentle river dragon, curls beneath a pavilion as distant festival drums unsettle her and Rook asks to speak from a visible safe distance.

pages.text: Willow explained that she loved the festival but could not sleep beside its loudest stage. The organizers had a sheltered garden farther from the speakers. They asked the gardeners whether it could host her and whether the visitors’ path should change. Rook carried the agreed messages instead of announcing that a dragon would simply move in. The gardeners proposed hours that worked for everyone.
pages.scene: Rook carries a request between festival organizers and gardeners while Willow waits beside the pavilion, with a sheltered garden visible beyond the busy stage.

pages.text: Lin marked the alternate footpath while stewards helped Willow reach her new resting place. The dragon folded herself carefully away from the beds. Rook left a clear sign with the gardeners’ chosen words, and a child added a picture of a sleeping cloud. Willow chuckled at it before settling down. Her tail stayed out of the path, and the afternoon concert continued.
pages.scene: Willow rests without disturbing plants in the sheltered garden as Lin marks a public detour and Rook places a child’s sleeping-cloud sign beside the entrance.

pages.text: In the evening Willow returned to listen to the softer music from a comfortable distance. She thanked the gardeners and helped carry their empty folding chairs with permission. Rook recorded a tale of neighbors adjusting a shared space, not of a bird taming a beast. Willow read the account and asked him to include that she had enjoyed the final song. He gave it a whole sentence.
pages.scene: Willow enjoys quiet evening music beside the gardeners and Rook, with folded chairs and a reviewed story account resting near the pavilion.

chapters.title: The moon gate
chapters.theme: A glimpse is not permission to enter
chapters.summary: An inviting garden view needs boundaries its hosts can explain.

pages.text: Rook saw a circular doorway framing a lovely small garden and stepped toward it with his atlas open. A caretaker named Yu welcomed him to the public courtyard but asked him to stop at the next gate. Beyond it, residents were having a private meal. The round opening made a beautiful view. It did not turn the people inside into part of a visitor’s exhibit.
pages.scene: Rook pauses at a circular garden doorway as Yu indicates the boundary between a public courtyard and a private meal beyond the next gate.

pages.text: Rook closed his sketchbook and apologized. Yu showed him a public garden plan with a suggested path and explained which spaces opened at different hours. He asked whether visitors needed clearer signs, and Rook described the mistake he had made without blaming the doorway. They invited a few neighbors to test the plan, including someone arriving for the first time.
pages.scene: Yu and Rook review a public garden plan with residents and a first-time visitor at a courtyard desk, leaving the private gate closed.

pages.text: The neighbors chose a small notice that felt like a welcome rather than a scolding. It named the shared areas and offered a way to ask about special visits. Rook sketched only the empty public courtyard after receiving permission. A resident who did not want to appear in the drawing passed behind him without explanation. The drawing needed a garden, not every person in it.
pages.scene: Rook sketches the empty public courtyard beside a small welcome notice while a resident passes privately beyond the frame and Yu watches the agreed path.

pages.text: Later Yu invited him to a community supper in the garden. Rook entered as a guest, with his notebook tucked away. The round gate looked exactly as beautiful as before, and the invitation made the evening richer. He left with the hosts’ chosen recipe note and no pictures of their private meal. A place could open generously because its people could also decide when to close.
pages.scene: Rook joins an invited community supper with his atlas closed in his satchel, framed by the round garden gate and warm evening lights.

chapters.title: The kite that came down
chapters.theme: A smaller safe choice can be the joyful one
chapters.summary: A child’s kite changes course when the wind changes.

pages.text: A young fox named Jun made a kite shaped like a paper boat and invited Rook to its first flight. Rook loved how it rose above the riverside field. Then the wind turned, carrying it toward a crowded walkway. Jun wanted to keep it flying because she had worked all week. Rook remembered the bridge that waited and suggested asking the field steward about the new wind.
pages.scene: Jun and Rook watch a paper-boat kite change direction above a riverside field as a steward observes the crowded walkway nearby.

pages.text: The steward helped Jun bring the kite down within the field’s safe area. One corner had creased. Jun sat beside it, furious at the lost flight. Rook did not tell her to be grateful for a lesson. He sat with her until she was ready to talk, then asked whether she wanted help carrying it home or time to think about another way to enjoy the afternoon.
pages.scene: Jun sits beside her safely lowered creased kite while Rook offers quiet company and the steward keeps the field boundary clear.

pages.text: Jun chose the covered workshop, where Mei had spare paper for visitors. She made a tiny version of the boat kite that could hang over her desk. Rook made a harbor bird that looked comically unlike himself. They laughed at its enormous beak. The larger kite would wait for suitable conditions; the small paper fleet could sail above a table while the wind did whatever it wished outside.
pages.scene: Jun and Rook make tiny hanging paper boats and an awkward large-beaked bird at Mei’s workshop while the full-sized kite rests safely against a wall.

pages.text: Two days later, the steward confirmed that the field was ready for another flight. Jun chose a modest height and brought the kite down before the afternoon changed. She had a fine flight and a fine paper boat at home. Rook put neither above the other in his account. Joy could take more than one shape, including one that fit the day it had been given.
pages.scene: Jun flies her repaired boat kite at a modest height in the open field while Rook watches and a small paper boat peeks from her bag.
pages.prop: A flight that fits the day

chapters.title: The two ferries
chapters.theme: A route remains useful when its alternatives are clear
chapters.summary: Shen helps waiting passengers choose rather than guess.

pages.text: Shen operated the small ferry linking the printing street to the opposite quay. One morning it needed maintenance, and passengers gathered beneath its timetable. Rook offered to announce that the larger ferry downstream would take everyone. Shen asked him to check its route and capacity first. It reached a different landing, and some passengers could not use the long stair from there.
pages.scene: Passengers gather by Shen’s paused ferry timetable while Rook and Shen compare the downstream ferry’s landing and stairway on a public map.

pages.text: Shen contacted the other ferry’s crew and the riverside shuttle. The team posted the checked options, including a step-free route and expected waiting times that could change. Rook stood beside the board to read it aloud for anyone who asked. A passenger chose to wait for the repair rather than take a longer journey. Rook respected that decision without calling it the wrong answer.
pages.scene: Shen and Rook post verified ferry and step-free shuttle options; passengers choose from the clear board rather than crowding around guesses.

pages.text: The repair crew found that the small ferry needed more time. Shen updated the board instead of leaving the earlier estimate in place. The passenger who had chosen to wait changed her mind and took the shuttle. Rook walked her to its marked stop. Nothing about her earlier choice had been foolish; a new fact had made another route a better fit.
pages.scene: Rook guides a passenger to the marked shuttle stop as Shen updates the waiting-time board and the maintenance crew continues its checks.

pages.text: By afternoon the ferry returned to service after its crew’s checks. Shen kept the alternate-route card on the notice board for future disruptions. Rook crossed with him and watched the two landings from the water. A city did not need every route to work every moment to care for its travelers. It needed honest updates and options people could actually use.
pages.scene: Rook and Shen cross the river aboard the checked ferry while an alternate-route card remains on the quay notice board behind them.

chapters.title: The roof garden
chapters.theme: New places can carry old friendships
chapters.summary: A modern city rooftop makes space for a garden conversation.

pages.text: Mei invited Rook to a community roof garden above a busy apartment building. He had expected every memorable place in the river world to be an old pavilion. Instead an elevator opened onto planters, a weather board, and neighbors talking beside a solar-powered light. Lin laughed at his surprised face. “People keep making places to meet,” she said. “We did not stop when your story began.”
pages.scene: An elevator opens onto a contemporary roof garden with planters, a weather board, and a small solar-powered light as Mei and Lin greet surprised Rook.

pages.text: A planter delivery had arrived at the wrong entrance. Rook offered to carry the heavy boxes upstairs, but the building coordinator had a safe delivery process. He helped check the labels and guide the delivery team to the correct service point instead. The neighbors chose where their new plants would go. Rook shared Nima’s garden sketch as a conversation piece, with its permission and credits intact.
pages.scene: Rook checks planter labels with the building coordinator while a delivery team uses the approved service route and neighbors study Nima’s credited garden sketch.

pages.text: One neighbor preferred a shaded reading corner to another row of pots. Another wanted space for children to draw. The garden group found room for both by changing a movable table’s position. Rook asked before sketching the scene and left people out if they wished. The most interesting feature of the roof was not its height. It was how its neighbors kept negotiating a shared place.
pages.scene: Neighbors rearrange a movable table between a shaded reading corner and children’s drawing space while Rook sketches only agreed details of the roof garden.

pages.text: That night the small light glowed above the table, and Mei sent a permitted picture of the garden to Sima. Rook added the roof to his atlas beside the covered bridge, giving both their own dates and stories. Old skills and new meeting places could share a page without becoming the same thing. From the roof, the northbound station shone across the city.
pages.scene: Mei and Rook sit under the roof garden’s small light with a permitted photograph and atlas page, while the city’s northbound station glows beyond.

chapters.title: The northbound window
chapters.theme: A farewell can carry an invitation onward
chapters.summary: Rook boards a train with a new letter and a quieter travel plan.

pages.text: At the northbound station, Mei handed Rook a letter for Dasha, keeper of the Snowbound Library. Lin gave him a permitted copy of the bridge story, including the apprentice’s correction. Rook checked the train number with the station staff instead of following a painted bird that merely looked familiar. His friends waited with him until the announced platform was ready.
pages.scene: Mei and Lin give Rook a sealed letter and credited bridge account at a busy northbound station while staff confirm the correct platform.

pages.text: A family entered the quiet carriage with a child who was overwhelmed by the station noise. Rook’s lantern handle clinked every time he moved, so he wrapped it with a spare cloth after asking the crew where it belonged. He put his notebook away and enjoyed the view. Being useful on this part of the journey meant taking up a little less sound.
pages.scene: Rook secures his brass lantern quietly in a passenger carriage as a family settles nearby and the station recedes beyond the window.

pages.text: The train paused while the crew waited for a cleared route ahead. Rook’s fellow passengers asked how long it would take. He directed them to the official announcement rather than inventing an answer from the trees outside. A boy wanted a story, so Rook quietly told him about Jun’s paper fleet. The child made a boat from his own scrap paper and kept it on the table.
pages.scene: Passengers wait calmly inside a stopped train as Rook points toward the official notice and a boy folds a small paper boat beside the window.
pages.prop: A paper boat on the train

pages.text: Snow appeared far beyond the next mountains. At the announced station, Dasha greeted Rook with an ordinary warm coat and a smile. He handed over Mei’s unopened letter. “I have heard about a library that keeps travelers’ stories,” he said. Dasha took his satchel only after he agreed. “Then you have arrived at a good door.” Behind them, the train carried its other journeys onward.
pages.scene: Dasha welcomes Rook at a snowy station, accepting Mei’s unopened letter while the northbound train prepares to continue beyond the mountains.

worlds.title: The Snowbound Library
worlds.region: A fictional winter journey inspired by Russia’s varied landscapes and storytelling traditions
worlds.tagline: Keep a warm place for the next traveler.
worlds.description: Rook visits one invented northern community during winter, not an entire country frozen into one season. Dasha’s library, Anya’s workshop, Misha’s bakery, and a passenger railway hold stories of hospitality, care, and honest routes. An original runaway-loaf adventure nods to the broader folktale tradition.
worlds.travel: A train brings Rook to the winter library; a checked coastal passenger ship carries him west toward the Wide-Sky Commons.

chapters.title: The warm door
chapters.theme: Let a host tell you what welcome looks like
chapters.summary: Dasha’s winter library gives Rook warmth without asking him to perform gratitude.

pages.text: Snow brushed Rook’s scarf as Dasha led him from the station to a timber library. A sign offered warm seats to travelers during opening hours. Inside, a kettle hummed and someone repaired a modern tablet at a side desk. Rook had expected a place made only of old stories. Dasha smiled. “We read yesterday, today, and tomorrow here. Which seat would you like?”
pages.scene: Dasha welcomes Rook into a timber library with a kettle, warm seats, books, and a visitor repairing a tablet at a side desk.

pages.text: Rook chose a place near the window and admitted that his bird feet were cold. Dasha found felt boots in the travelers’ loan basket and an earflap hat that kept his red face visible. She asked whether they fit before he wore them. They were useful borrowed clothes, not a costume he had to perform to belong. Rook thanked her and carefully noted where to return them.
pages.scene: Rook tries borrowed felt boots and an earflap hat with his red swept crest still visible while Dasha checks the fit beside a travelers’ loan basket.

pages.text: Dasha read Mei’s letter and placed Lin’s permitted bridge account on the exchange shelf. A child asked if Rook had really come from a book. “That is how I remember it,” he answered. “I cannot tell you who drew the first page.” The child accepted that and showed him a drawing of a library with wheels. They imagined where such a library might travel.
pages.scene: Dasha reads Mei’s introduction as a child shows Rook an imaginative wheeled-library drawing near the exchange shelf holding Lin’s credited account.

pages.text: When evening arrived, Dasha explained the library’s closing time and helped Rook find his arranged guest room. He did not mistake a warm public seat for a promise that every door would remain open forever. The guest-room window looked back toward the library lamp. Rook wrote to Lumen that he had found another good door, and a host who let him be both grateful and tired.
pages.scene: Rook writes to Lumen from an arranged guest room, with borrowed boots drying safely by the door and the library lamp visible through the window.

chapters.title: The loaf that chose to stop
chapters.theme: A familiar story can leave room for a new decision
chapters.summary: A talking little loaf discovers that stopping is a choice too.

pages.text: Misha the baker set a round loaf on the windowsill, and in this story the loaf promptly blinked. He named himself Bun and rolled toward the lane, singing a song he had just invented. Rook recognized the shape of a traveling folktale, but Bun’s words were his own. “Where will you go?” Rook asked. “Farther,” Bun replied, which was not quite an address.
pages.scene: A small original talking loaf named Bun blinks on Misha’s bakery windowsill while Rook watches the snowy lane beyond the open window.

pages.text: Bun rolled safely into the cleared yard, then saw a steep lane ahead. Rook suggested stopping to decide, but Bun worried that every good traveling story required more traveling. Dasha arrived with a tray. “A book may have an ending,” she said, “but you can make a choice before reaching it.” Bun rested on the tray and listened to the quiet inside the bakery.
pages.scene: Bun pauses on Dasha’s tray beside the bakery yard as Rook points out a steep lane and warm light shines from the shop.

pages.text: Misha asked whether Bun wanted to return, stay in the library window, or travel later with a companion. Bun chose a library visit first. Dasha carried him in a safe basket, and Rook walked beside her. They did not sing another storyteller’s refrain. Bun composed a new verse about asking where the next road led and being allowed to change his mind.
pages.scene: Dasha carries Bun in a secure basket toward the library as Rook walks beside her and Misha waves from the bakery door.
